items.readable_text:
Content:
When we factor a linear expression, we rewrite it as a product.

Content:
A common situation is when two terms share a greatest common factor (GCF).
To factor, we do two steps:

Content:
1. Write each term as a product using the GCF.
2. Pull the GCF out in front of parentheses.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's factor the expression [MATH: 32x + 12.]

Content:
1. First, find the greatest common factor: [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(32x,12)=4.] Since [MATH: 32x = 4 \cdot 8x] and [MATH: 12 = 4\cdot 3,] we separate that factor from each term as follows:
[MATH: 32x + 12|=; (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)]
2. Now the factor [MATH: 4] is common to both terms, so we place it in front of the parentheses:
[MATH: (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|=; 4_(⏟)_(GCF)(8x + 3)]

Content:
After factoring, we can check our work by using the distributive law on [MATH: 4(8x+3)] to get back [MATH: 32x+12.]

sections.normalized_html:
We factor in two steps:

  1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms. In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(32x, 12) = 4,] so [MATH: 32x + 12|=; (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|.]

  2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses: [MATH: (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|=; 4(8x + 3)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 4(8x+3).]

items.title: Factoring a Difference of Two Linear Expressions

sections.normalized_html:
We factor in two steps:

  1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms (ignoring any negative signs). In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(63x,36) = 9,] so: [MATH: 63x − 36|=; (9 ⋅ 7x) − (9 ⋅ 4)]

  2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses: [MATH: (9 ⋅ 7x) − (9 ⋅ 4)|=; 9(7x − 4)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 9(7x-4).]

items.title: Factoring Expressions With More Than Two Terms

sections.normalized_html:
We factor in two steps:

  1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms (ignoring any negative signs). In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(4x,20y,12) = 4,] so [MATH: 4x + 20y − 12|=; (4 ⋅ x) + (4 ⋅ 5y) − (4 ⋅ 3).]

  2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses: [MATH: (4 ⋅ x) + (4 ⋅ 5y) − (4 ⋅ 3)|=; 4(x + 5y − 3)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 4(x + 5y - 3).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When we factor a linear expression, we rewrite it as a product.

Content:
A common situation is when two terms share a greatest common factor (GCF).
To factor, we do two steps:

Content:
1. Write each term as a product using the GCF.
2. Pull the GCF out in front of parentheses.

Content:
To demonstrate, let's factor the expression [MATH: 32x + 12.]

Content:
1. First, find the greatest common factor: [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(32x,12)=4.] Since [MATH: 32x = 4 \cdot 8x] and [MATH: 12 = 4\cdot 3,] we separate that factor from each term as follows:
[MATH: 32x + 12|=; (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)]

[MATH: (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|=; 4_(⏟)_(GCF)(8x + 3)]

Content:
After factoring, we can check our work by using the distributive law on [MATH: 4(8x+3)] to get back [MATH: 32x+12.]

Item 2 — Example: Factoring A Sum of Two Linear Expressions

Example Prompt:

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We factor in two steps:

1. Separate the greatest common factor from each of the terms. In this case, [MATH: \textrm{GCF}(32x, 12) = 4,] so
[MATH: 32x + 12|=; (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|.]
2. Place the common factor in front of the parentheses, leaving whatever remains inside the parentheses:
[MATH: (4 ⋅ 8x) + (4 ⋅ 3)|=; 4(8x + 3)]

Thus, the factored form of the expression is [MATH: 4(8x+3).]
